The two paths share the constant construction and finalization architecture, so the example is not an independent proof of the formula for π\pi. The enclosure’s mathematical justification comes from the builder’s documented construction; release qualification supplies additional finite tests. Keep those kinds of evidence distinct when describing results to users.

7.6 How the constant builders justify their bounds

The constant implementations use exact integer or rational construction together with outward rounding. The π\pi builder uses a Chudnovsky series and exact binary splitting. Its enclosure accounts for the omitted series tail and the rounding steps used in the scaled result. The natural-logarithm constant uses an exact series derived from

log2=2atanh(1/3). \log 2=2\operatorname{atanh}(1/3).

The finite sum is paired with a bound for the positive remainder, then converted outward to dyadic endpoints. Euler’s and Catalan’s constants use their documented series and asymptotic interval machinery. The common finalizer does not accept a result merely because the last two approximations agree.

These descriptions explain why an enclosure is available; they are not a substitute for the detailed derivations and implementation reviews. A client usually needs to rely on the public contract, retain the actual exported endpoints when reproducibility matters, and avoid presenting a finite validation suite as a universal theorem about every execution environment.

7.7 Caches retain reusable mathematical information

A constant cache stores a certified interval, allowing it to serve different destination precisions and rounding modes. It does not merely store a nearest-rounded number and reuse that number as if it were exact. A separate rounded-result cache may answer a repeated request more cheaply.

This makes precomputation useful when many calls will request the same constants. ppf_precompute_constant and the constant-specific precompute functions allow the application to arrange that work before a latency-sensitive phase. A higher-precision cached enclosure can also help later lower-precision requests. The cache-precision query reports cache state; it is not a certificate for an unrelated expression that uses the constant.

Cache construction and access are synchronized. Clearing a cache deliberately discards reusable work. Reserve explicit cache cleanup for a lifecycle boundary, controlled benchmark, or memory policy rather than clearing it after every call in a repeated numerical workload. The small standalone example clears caches at exit to demonstrate complete cleanup.

Worker-count entry points allow parallel construction where the implementation supports it. A worker request is not a promise of a speedup. Initialization, synchronization, cache hits, problem size, and the selected algorithm affect actual cost. When reporting timing, distinguish cold construction from a warm lookup and record precision, mode, worker policy, and cache state.

7.8 A certificate needs an enclosure argument

ppf_set_dyadic_interval validates and rounds the interval supplied by the caller. It cannot establish that an arbitrary interval encloses the mathematical quantity the application has in mind. If a program supplies bounds around a poor approximation without a justified error estimate, a decided result certifies only the decision implied by those supplied bounds.

For a complete application-level certificate, record the target quantity, exact input interpretation, derivation of the bounds, endpoint integers and exponent, destination precision, rounding mode, and interval decision. Include the output ternary and relevant flags if these are part of the claimed result. A rounded decimal rendering can accompany this record for readability, but it should not replace the exact endpoints.

This discipline is especially useful when composing several operations. Each successful scalar call concerns its own exact stored inputs. An enclosure for a complete expression must propagate input uncertainty and intermediate bounds through that expression. The library gives the application reliable building blocks; the application must still connect them to the mathematical question it is answering.

8 Elementary functions without avoidable information loss

Choosing a mathematically equivalent formula can change the accuracy and cost of a floating-point calculation. A dedicated log1p call preserves a small increment that would disappear if the program first formed a rounded 1+x. A scaled-angle function preserves an exact turn fraction that would be perturbed by multiplying by a rounded value of π\pi. These are choices about the problem presented to the library, not merely about the number of guard bits used internally.

The complete program numeric_elementary.c demonstrates both effects. It uses exact dyadic inputs, explicit nearest rounding, and a 53-bit destination, making the examples independent of decimal input conversion.

8.1 Start with the intended expression

The elementary families include natural, base-two, and base-ten logarithms; exponentials and their small-increment forms; integer and general powers; trigonometric functions; inverse angles; and hyperbolic functions. The most useful first question is whether the family already contains a function that expresses the mathematical quantity directly.

Intended quantity Prefer Avoid forming first when accuracy matters
log(1+x)\log(1+x) for small xx ppf_log1p A destination-rounded 1+x
exp(x)−1\exp(x)-1 for small xx ppf_expm1 A destination-rounded exponential
log2(1+x)\log_2(1+x) ppf_log2p1 A rounded sum followed by ppf_log2
2x−12^x-1 ppf_exp2m1 A rounded power followed by subtraction
(1+x)n(1+x)^n with integer nn ppf_compound_si A prematurely rounded increment
sin(πx)\sin(\pi x) ppf_sinpi Multiplication by a rounded constant
sin(2πx/u)\sin(2\pi x/u) ppf_sinu Conversion of an exact turn fraction to radians

The dedicated functions keep the defining expression inside their numerical evaluation. This gives them an opportunity to preserve relationships that would already be lost in a sequence of public calls. It does not make the external input exact if the application originally imported an approximation.

8.2 A tiny increment can vanish before the logarithm starts

At 53-bit precision, the spacing immediately above one is 2−522^{-52}. Take the exactly represented input

x=2−80. x=2^{-80}.

It is far smaller than half that spacing. Nearest rounding of 1+x therefore produces exactly one. A subsequent call to ppf_log correctly returns zero for the input it actually receives. The logarithm has not made a mistake; the addition changed the question.

ppf_log1p receives the original dyadic xx and evaluates the combined expression. Its result remains positive. ppf_expm1 similarly preserves the small positive difference between exp(x)\exp(x) and one.

The example prints:

log of the rounded 1 + 2^-80 is zero at 53 bits.
log1p(2^-80) and expm1(2^-80) remain positive.
sinpi(1) is exactly zero; sin of rounded pi is not.

The positive result may still be inexact. Positivity, representability, and exactness are different properties. The example checks the property relevant to the cancellation problem instead of interpreting every nonzero ternary as failure.

Increasing only the logarithm destination precision cannot undo the first addition’s rounding. To recompute the original expression at greater precision, rebuild the inputs and intermediate steps whose information was lost. A higher-precision container holding the same rounded one still represents one.

8.3 Preserve exact angle structure

Ordinary ppf_sin, ppf_cos, and ppf_tan take angles in radians. Their input is the exact stored binary number. If the program obtains an approximation pi from ppf_const_pi, then calls ppf_sin(pi), it asks for the sine of that binary approximation. Since the approximation is not the mathematical constant π\pi, the result need not be zero.

ppf_sinpi(x) means sin(πx)\sin(\pi x). The factor of π\pi is part of the function definition, so the implementation can recognize integer and other exact grid cases before ordinary numerical reduction. At x=1x=1, the result is exactly zero. This is the third observation checked by the example.

For degrees, an exact unit-scaled input can be particularly convenient: ppf_sinu(x,360,...) represents sin(2πx/360)\sin(2\pi x/360). For a system that counts phase in turns, use a consistent exact turn scale. The unit parameter is part of the API’s domain and must satisfy its documented requirements; do not substitute a native rounded conversion constant when an exact integer scale is available.

Large angles deserve an input-quality check. A binary value of large magnitude can have many significant bits while still having little resolution in its fractional-turn position. Accurate range reduction computes the function of that stored value. It cannot determine which nearby physical angle was intended if measurement or import discarded the needed low bits.

8.4 Inverse angles and quadrants

Use ppf_atan2 when both Cartesian coordinates are available and the quadrant matters. Computing an ordinary quotient and passing it to ppf_atan can lose quadrant information, can encounter division by zero unnecessarily, and introduces an intermediate rounding. The two-argument function has explicit rules for axes, signed zeros, infinities, and NaNs.

Scaled inverse-angle variants return answers in the corresponding π\pi or unit convention. They are useful when the caller ultimately wants a turn fraction rather than radians. State the convention in interfaces and stored data; the same numerical value can mean a different angle under a different scale.

For asin and acos, check that a real input is in [-1,1]. A dot product of nominal unit vectors can drift slightly outside this interval after earlier rounding or because the vectors were not exactly normalized. Silently clamping the input changes the mathematical problem. If the application intentionally clamps to accommodate a known modeling tolerance, document that tolerance and retain the original residual for diagnosis.

A similar distinction applies to atanh: the finite real interior is (-1,1), with poles at the endpoints. acosh has a real domain beginning at one. A domain check should compare the actual ppf_t value, not a conversion to double that can round a nearby out-of-domain value back onto the boundary.

8.5 Integer powers and general powers have different information

When the exponent is an integer in the application’s model, pass it through an integer-power interface such as ppf_pow_ui, ppf_pow_si, or ppf_pow_z, according to its representation. This retains exact parity and avoids treating a rounded floating exponent as if it were the intended integer.

A general negative base has a real result for integer exponents, with sign determined by parity. The expression (−8)1/3(-8)^{1/3} illustrates a different issue: a finite binary approximation to one third is not exactly one third. A general real-power call with that exponent does not communicate the intention “take the real cube root.” Use ppf_cbrt or an appropriate integer-degree root function when that is the intended operation.

ppf_powr has a stricter domain than ppf_pow. It is not simply an alternative spelling. In particular, cases involving a negative base or ambiguous zero/infinity exponents follow its documented invalid-value rules. Choose the function based on the mathematical convention needed by the application, then handle its special values explicitly.

Some noninteger powers are exact, such as 91/2=39^{1/2}=3 and 811/4=381^{1/4}=3. The implementation contains exact-case routes so that a numerical enclosure need not be forced to prove equality by indefinitely narrowing around a representable answer. An application should still inspect the returned ternary rather than infer exactness from a familiar-looking decimal rendering.

8.6 What the internal enclosure establishes

For nontrivial cases, the implementation constructs directed bounds at a working precision, attempts to settle the requested output, and refines when the decision remains ambiguous. Depending on the function and argument, the first path may use fixed-point integer endpoints or floating interval objects. The public meaning is the requested function of the exact stored inputs, rounded to the destination precision and mode.

For a deterministic rounding mode, a completed endpoint decision includes the value and the applicable rounding direction and range information. Merely obtaining identical nearest-rounded approximations at two working precisions would not establish these facts. The library’s certificate-oriented paths therefore use enclosure finalization rather than a “digits stopped changing” test.

There are still finite implementation limits. Iteration counts, workspace sizes, transformed-argument alignment, and available memory constrain execution. The current logarithm/exponential interval layer caps a particular dyadic alignment step at 1,000,000 bits. This is a workspace bound on that representation step, not a universal limit on input precision or exponent. An exact shortcut or a proved saturation path may avoid it; another request can be rejected before an enormous temporary is allocated.

A representation or certification rejection returns the documented error sentinel and status flags. Repeating the same request without changing its representation or work policy is not a general remedy. Nor should an application remove a guard simply to obtain an unchecked approximation. Record which function and inputs failed, then choose an explicitly supported alternative formulation or report the limitation to the caller.

8.7 Compose functions with a clear error model

Successful scalar calls do not automatically give a final expression the same single-rounding contract. For example, log(x) followed by multiplication by y, followed by exp, introduces visible intermediate roundings. ppf_pow(x,y) can keep those stages inside one evaluation of the power. Both programs can be useful, but they answer different floating-point specifications.

For an application-level bound, use directed operations and valid interval formulas throughout. Monotone functions allow endpoint propagation only on a domain where the monotonicity assertion holds. Sine over an interval spanning a maximum cannot be bounded by evaluating just its two endpoints. Division requires a denominator interval that avoids zero, or a more elaborate treatment of the singularity.

For an application-level approximation, record input precision and the complete formula, perform a precision study, and describe the result as observed stability unless an error bound has been proved. This distinction is useful even in ordinary engineering work: it tells the next reader whether the uncertainty is from input data, numerical rounding, or an unresolved mathematical bound.

9 Special functions and difficult domains

Special functions often expose a gap between a formula that exists mathematically and a numerical request that can be completed economically. Poles, sign changes, cancellation, large parameters, and finite implementation bounds all affect how an application should use the interface. A useful wrapper must distinguish these cases instead of reporting every unusual outcome as “not enough precision.”

The complete program numeric_special_domains.c demonstrates four different situations: an exact Gamma value, a finite logarithmic magnitude with a separate sign, a real-domain NaN, and an explicit practical-domain rejection. These are representative calling patterns, not a claim that the example covers every special-function branch.

9.1 Choose the quantity and its convention

The special-function surface includes the Gamma family, beta, zeta, exponential integral, dilogarithm, error functions, Bessel functions of integer order, the arithmetic–geometric mean, and Airy Ai. Consult the function’s mathematical convention before replacing a formula from another library. Similar names can refer to a logarithm, a normalized quantity, or a different branch.

Interface Quantity or convention
ppf_gamma Real Gamma function, with documented poles and special values
ppf_lgamma log|Γ(x)|\log|\Gamma(x)|, plus a separate Gamma sign output
ppf_lngamma Real logΓ(x)\log\Gamma(x), where Gamma is positive
ppf_digamma Logarithmic derivative of Gamma
ppf_gamma_inc Upper incomplete Gamma function
ppf_beta Beta function with the implementation’s stated real-domain rules
ppf_erf, ppf_erfc Error function and complementary error function
ppf_jn, ppf_yn Bessel functions of integer order
ppf_ai Airy Ai, subject to a practical finite-argument limit

For positive shape and nonnegative lower limit, the upper incomplete Gamma convention is

Γ(a,x)=∫x∞ta−1e−tdt. \Gamma(a,x)=\int_x^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt.

It is not the lower integral from zero to xx, and it is not automatically divided by Γ(a)\Gamma(a). If a probability formula needs a regularized ratio, that normalization is part of the application’s expression and error analysis. The implementation also has real-parameter continuation paths; their existence should not be read as an unrestricted promise of cheap completion for every extreme parameter.

9.2 Gamma: magnitude and sign are separate information

For positive integers, Γ(n)=(n−1)!\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!. The example uses the exactly representable input five and verifies that the 80-bit result is exactly 24 with zero ternary. This is a useful sanity check, but it is much easier than evaluating a point close to a negative-integer pole.

For negative nonintegral arguments, Gamma changes sign between poles. At x=−1/2x=-1/2,

Γ(−1/2)=−2π. \Gamma(-1/2)=-2\sqrt{\pi}.

Its absolute value has a finite real logarithm. ppf_lgamma therefore provides a finite logarithmic magnitude and a separate sign of -1. ppf_lngamma cannot return a real logarithm of that negative value and reports a numerical NaN under its real-domain convention.

These outcomes are not interchangeable. Exponentiating the magnitude returned by lgamma loses the Gamma sign unless the application restores it. Treat the auxiliary sign as part of the result, validate it only after a successful call, and preserve it with the numerical output when storing or passing the result onward.

For large positive arguments, a logarithmic representation often avoids an otherwise unnecessary overflow. An application computing ratios of large Gamma values may benefit from a logarithmic formulation, but cancellation in the difference of logarithms still needs analysis. Subtracting two separately rounded large logarithms is not automatically equivalent to one certified beta or ratio evaluation.

9.3 Poles and nearby points require exact input awareness

A negative integer and a nearby negative noninteger can produce radically different Gamma behavior. The distinction must be made using the stored high-precision value. Converting it to a native floating type for an “is this an integer?” check can destroy the very offset that distinguishes the two cases.

The same principle applies when generating a point near a pole. If the intended input is −n+2−k-n+2^{-k}, construct that dyadic expression at sufficient precision. Writing a long decimal number through a native double temporary may round it to −n-n. A correctly rounded special-function result for the rounded integer would then answer the wrong input question.

Increasing output precision does not repair that change. Reconstruct the original input from its exact integer/rational description or original text at the new precision. Record whether a test is probing the mathematical pole itself, a representable neighboring value, or a decimal value rounded onto one of those points.

A wrapper should classify NaN and infinity explicitly. A documented pole may return an infinity and set a division-by-zero flag without returning PPF_TERNARY_ERROR. A real-domain invalid value may return NaN and set the NaN flag. These are specified numerical outcomes, while the sentinel identifies a request that did not produce its ordinary requested result.

9.4 A practical bound is different from a mathematical domain

Airy Ai is mathematically meaningful for every finite real argument. The current implementation nevertheless restricts its ordinary finite-input evaluation to |x|≤500|x|\le500. A finite argument outside that interval produces PPF_TERNARY_ERROR with PPF_FLAG_ERANGE. This is an implementation boundary, not a claim that Ai is undefined there.

The bound is checked on the exact stored input. A number slightly greater than 500 remains out of range even if conversion to double or long double would round it back to 500. Applications that validate this boundary should therefore use the library comparison functions, as the example does with ppf_cmpabs_ui.

The example deliberately calls Ai at 501 after identifying that the input exceeds the supported interval. It verifies the documented rejection and checks that no project-allocation failure was reported. Its output is:

Gamma(5) = 24 exactly.
lgamma(-1/2) returns a finite log magnitude and sign -1.
lngamma(-1/2) reports a real-domain NaN.
Ai(501) exceeds the implementation domain: ERANGE, not ALLOC.

An application would normally turn the same precheck into a clear user-facing message or choose a different supported method. The example makes the rejected call so that the distinction between numerical range status and allocation failure is executable and reviewable.

Integer-order Bessel evaluation has another explicit practical bound: the general nontrivial jn and yn paths reject order magnitude above 100,000. Special inputs can be resolved before that work is needed. Even below the bound, a large order or argument can be expensive. A numeric cutoff is not a promise of uniform running time throughout the accepted region.

For upper incomplete Gamma at a finite positive lower limit, the negative-shape recurrence admits shape parameters a≥−100000a\ge-100000. A smaller shape is rejected before converting it into a recurrence count. The special cases at a zero or infinite lower limit are handled separately. This is another practical recurrence bound, not the mathematical domain of the defining integral for positive lower limit. Exact-case recognition can avoid some expensive general routes: for example, negative even integer zeta inputs can be recognized from their compact dyadic representation without materializing an enormous integer.

9.5 Complementary functions and cancellation

When the desired quantity is a small complementary tail, prefer its dedicated interface. For example, evaluating erf(x) and subtracting its rounded value from one can erase a small erfc(x) value. A direct complementary-function call keeps the defining relationship within the evaluator and avoids this particular external rounding step.

The same caution applies to incomplete Gamma formulas assembled from a complete Gamma value minus a lower contribution. Such differences can be much smaller than either term. A formula that is algebraically correct can be numerically fragile if its terms are rounded independently before subtraction.

Near a zero of an oscillatory special function, absolute error and relative error tell very different stories. A small absolute uncertainty can correspond to a large relative uncertainty when the true value is near zero. Choose the accuracy measure that matters to the application. If the sign near a root is important, seek an interval that excludes zero rather than assuming that a displayed nonzero decimal digit proves the sign.

9.6 Certification rejection and allocation rollback

The special-function evaluators use finite working-precision schedules and bounded internal algorithms. An unresolved enclosure, an unsupported practical domain, or an internal representation limit can cause an ordinary numerical rejection. The error sentinel tells the application not to use the destination as a newly computed answer. It does not, by itself, promise that the destination still contains its previous value.

The project-allocation contract is more specific. For the governed public transcendental and special-function entry points, an unrecovered failure of a configured Polyphase allocation raises the sticky allocation flag, returns the sentinel, and preserves initialized numerical destinations. Paired outputs commit together under that contract, and the lgamma auxiliary sign is protected with its numerical output. The staging machinery can distinguish a newly failed allocation from an allocation flag that was already sticky before the call.

A numerical rejection without a project-allocation failure may commit a staged NaN or other documented error result. Therefore, code that requires its previous numerical value after any unsuccessful request should arrange its own temporary destination and copy only after applying the application’s full success test. That test may include classification and domain policy in addition to the sentinel.

This allocation guarantee concerns project-controlled requests and valid initialized objects. It does not intercept GMP’s internal allocation behavior or promise recovery from process termination or invalid allocator callbacks. Keep those ownership boundaries visible in a service’s resource policy without conflating them with numerical correctness.

9.7 A useful failure-handling sequence

First decide whether the input belongs to the intended real domain and whether it satisfies known practical bounds. Then clear or save the relevant context flags, execute the operation, and check its return contract. If the result is numerical, classify it before treating it as a finite quantity. If the call fails, inspect whether a new allocation failure occurred and retain the original input description for diagnosis.

The response should fit the failure. Correct a mistaken domain convention rather than merely increasing precision. Reconstruct an input that lost its offset during import. Use a logarithmic quantity if the application actually needs a log magnitude. Report a practical-domain limit when the implementation rejects the requested region. Escalate working precision only when the algorithm and application have a justified refinement policy and a finite resource budget.

Tests should include ordinary values, exact cases, points near poles or zeros, practical-boundary neighbors, and invalid-domain cases. A comparison with an independent implementation is valuable evidence over the tested set. Agreement at a few convenient values does not establish all-input correctness or resource-independent completion. The manual examples are intentionally small; the release’s broader validation records state their own exact tested ranges and limitations.

10 Numerical recipes and reproducible results

A numerical recipe should say what its inputs mean, what result it promises, and how it decides that enough work has been done. This chapter connects the library’s arithmetic and interval interfaces to those application-level questions. The recipes distinguish three increasingly strong observations: a value was computed successfully, repeated calculations look stable, and a justified enclosure certifies a particular rounding decision.

Two complete programs accompany the discussion: numeric_import.c compares decimal text with a native floating input, and numeric_refinement.c certifies a 53-bit square root using an independently constructed exact interval. Both programs check their claims before printing their expected output.

10.1 Recipe: import the information you actually possess

Suppose a data file contains the decimal text 0.1. There are at least three different objects the application might intend:

  1. the exact rational number 1/101/10;
  2. the nearest binary value at a selected Polyphase precision;
  3. the binary value already stored in a native double.

These are related, but they are not identical. A binary floating-point number with finite precision cannot equal 1/101/10, because the reduced denominator contains a factor of five. A direct decimal parse can round that rational to the selected precision. Importing an existing native double instead preserves the native value, including its earlier rounding.

The import example assumes a 53-bit binary double, checks that platform condition, and creates two 256-bit destinations. It parses the text into one and imports the C literal through ppf_set_d into the other:

ppf_set_str(&decimal, "0.1", 10, PPF_RNDN, &ctx);
ppf_set_d(&native, 0.1, PPF_RNDN, &ctx);

These two calls have different return contracts. The complete program checks status zero for ppf_set_str. It checks exact ternary zero for this particular ppf_set_d, because the already-rounded native binary value fits exactly into 256 bits. That exact import does not mean the native input equals the intended decimal rational.

To compare errors without another floating approximation, the example exports both stored values to GMP rationals and subtracts the exact rational 1/101/10. It compares the absolute rational errors. The 256-bit decimal parse is closer, though still not exact. It then widens the native-import object to 512 bits and verifies that its rational value is unchanged.

Expected output:

Neither binary value is exactly 1/10.
The 256-bit decimal parse is closer to 1/10.
Widening the native import preserves its old value.

If the input is already a double supplied by another API, preserving that value may be precisely the right operation. The problem arises only when the program claims to have imported the original decimal or measured quantity more accurately than the available data allows. Keep original text or an exact integer/rational representation when later recomputation at higher precision is part of the workflow.

10.2 Recipe: separate computation precision from output formatting

Choose the computational precision before the calculation. Choose the number of display digits afterward, based on what the output is intended to communicate. Printing more digits does not add information, and printing fewer digits can hide a meaningful difference between two internal values.

For reproducibility, retain the binary value or an exact dyadic export in addition to a human-readable decimal string. ppf_get_z_2exp expresses a finite regular value as an integer times a power of two. That representation makes the stored value unambiguous. It is especially useful when a later reviewer must distinguish input rounding from algorithmic differences.

For user-facing results, avoid implying that all printed digits are independently established digits of the mathematical target. A formatter can accurately print a stored approximation whose input or modeling error is much larger than its last displayed digit. Report an error bound or uncertainty separately when one is available, and state how it was obtained.

10.3 Recipe: use precision refinement as a diagnostic

A practical precision study recomputes the entire expression at several precisions, for example 64, 128, and 256 bits. Recreate inputs from their original description at each stage. Reusing a low-precision intermediate after widening it defeats the purpose of the study.

Compare results at a common target precision or compare their exact difference. Otherwise the display itself can make unrelated outputs look equal or make harmless low-order changes look alarming. Record whether every call completed successfully, whether the result remained finite, and whether the same range policy was used.

Stability is useful evidence. It can reveal an accidental native conversion, insufficient precision in one intermediate, a cancellation problem, or an unexpected dependence on evaluation order. However, two calculations can share the same input error, formula defect, or biased approximation. Agreement at two precisions does not prove a correct final rounding decision.

Give an approximation-based algorithm a stopping rule that matches its claim. If the application only requires observed stability to a stated display tolerance, label that outcome accordingly and set a finite retry limit. If it requires a certified binary result, construct or obtain justified bounds and use a certification test. Increasing precision is a work strategy; the stopping test supplies the evidence.

10.4 Recipe: build an exact enclosure for a square root

The refinement example targets 2\sqrt2. For a positive integer scale kk, form the exact integer

R=2⋅22k=22k+1 R=2\cdot2^{2k}=2^{2k+1}

and use GMP integer square root with remainder to obtain

L=⌊R⌋. L=\lfloor\sqrt R\rfloor.

Because RR is a power of two with an odd exponent, it is not an integer square. Thus the returned remainder is positive and

L2<R<(L+1)2. L^2<R<(L+1)^2.

Taking positive square roots and dividing by 2k2^k proves

L2−k<2<(L+1)2−k. L2^{-k}<\sqrt2<(L+1)2^{-k}.

This is an enclosure argument, not an estimate inferred from agreement of approximations. It uses exact integer arithmetic and supplies endpoints whose width is exactly 2−k2^{-k}. The program checks the nonzero remainder explicitly rather than silently assuming that every future variant of the recipe has the same irrational target.

The central construction is short:

mpz_set_ui(radicand, 2);
mpz_mul_2exp(radicand, radicand, 2u * k);
mpz_sqrtrem(lower, remainder, radicand);
mpz_add_ui(upper, lower, 1);

ppf_interval_status_t s = ppf_set_dyadic_interval(
    &result, lower, upper, -(ppf_exp_t)k,
    PPF_RNDN, &ternary, &ctx);

The complete program supplies initialization, checks, a finite sequence of scales, and cleanup. It never treats a failed allocation or an interval error as an instruction to continue with unchecked bounds.

10.5 Recipe: refine until the requested decision is established

The destination stays at 53 bits throughout the square-root example. Only the enclosure scale changes. The program tries 8, 16, 32, 64, and, if necessary, 128 bits of fixed-point scale. This separates target precision from work used to establish the target result.

At the first three scales, the enclosure is too wide to settle the 53-bit request. The program verifies that the undecided call leaves its initial destination value and ternary marker unchanged. At scale 64, the enclosure determines the result and proves that the nearest 53-bit value is above the exact square root.

Expected output:

scale 8: refine
scale 16: refine
scale 32: refine
scale 64: certified 53-bit sqrt(2), rounded upward

Here “rounded upward” describes the sign of the result’s error under nearest rounding. It does not mean that the requested mode was PPF_RNDU. A nearest-rounded answer can lie on either side of its exact target; the ternary records which side was selected in this particular case.

If the finite scale schedule ends without a decision, the program exits unsuccessfully and says that it did not obtain its certificate. It does not promote the last approximation to a certified answer. An application can choose a larger schedule or a different enclosure method, but it should report the outcome actually established by the work it performed.

10.6 Recipe: record a certificate that another reader can inspect

For the square-root recipe, a compact reproducibility record consists of the exact target expression, scale kk, integer endpoints, endpoint exponent −k-k, target precision, rounding mode, interval status, ternary, and context range. The integer-square-root remainder supplies a direct check of the enclosure construction.

For a constant, the record can contain the exported enclosure and the constant identifier, together with the construction/validation provenance on which the enclosure relies. For a general expression, record how input intervals and intermediate bounds were propagated. A collection of endpoints without an enclosure argument is not yet a certificate for the intended mathematical expression.

A numerical report should also state its boundaries: tested input ranges, platform and dependency versions, random seed if sampling was used, any retry or resource cap, and whether an independent oracle was involved. These details let another reader reproduce a finite assertion without mistaking it for a universal result.

10.7 Recipe: preserve an application result across rejected requests

Applications sometimes need to keep the last accepted value while attempting a new calculation. Use a separate initialized temporary of the intended destination precision. Run the new calculation into that temporary, inspect the sentinel, numerical classification, and application-specific domain requirements, and copy into the persistent result only after acceptance.

This pattern complements the library’s allocation rollback guarantees. It also covers numerical rejections and domain outcomes for which retaining the old value is an application preference rather than an API guarantee. Keep an explicit validity or freshness marker: an unchanged value can be a valid old result while the current request remains unresolved.

For a service or long-running calculation, pair that marker with a concise diagnostic record: the operation, exact or original input description, requested precision and mode, flags, and reason for rejection. Avoid returning a plausible old number without saying that the new calculation failed. A useful numerical interface communicates both the value it has and the question that value actually answers.

11 Text, formatting, and binary interchange

Choose an output representation according to what the next reader needs. A person usually needs a short decimal result with a stated precision. A parser needs an unambiguous token and a checked conversion. A saved numerical object needs its value, precision, and special-value information preserved. These are different tasks, and the library provides separate interfaces for them.

Task Interface What to check
Read one complete string ppf_set_str Zero means success; a nonzero result means failure
Read a number at the beginning of a string ppf_strtofr Error sentinel, end pointer, and any flags of interest
Obtain radix digits and a separate exponent ppf_get_str Non-null returned pointer; release allocated output with ppf_free_str
Produce a presentation string ppf_snprintf or ppf_asprintf Negative result means failure; check truncation separately
Read or write one text token on a stream ppf_inp_str, ppf_out_str Nonzero byte count, then the stream’s error state when relevant
Save or restore a numerical object ppf_fpif_export, ppf_fpif_import Zero means success

11.1 Reading numbers deliberately

Use ppf_set_str for a configuration field that must contain exactly one number. It accepts leading and trailing white space, but rejects an unconsumed suffix. For example, "1.25" is a complete decimal input, while "1.25 volts" requires either application-level parsing or the prefix interface. An empty or white-space-only string is not a successful complete conversion. The destination must already be initialized.

if (ppf_set_str(&value, "1.25", 10, PPF_RNDN, &ctx) != 0) {
    /* Report an invalid or unsuccessful conversion. */
}

The return value here is a status, not the ternary rounding relation returned by arithmetic. Successful parsing can round the input to the destination’s precision. Inspect PPF_FLAG_INEXACT when the application needs to distinguish exact conversion from rounding, clearing the relevant context flag before the operation if earlier work must not affect that decision.

Use ppf_strtofr when a larger grammar follows the number. On return, compare the end pointer with the original input pointer to detect no conversion, then validate the remaining text. A successful prefix does not validate a unit, delimiter, or trailing field. Check PPF_TERNARY_ERROR separately before using the result. A pointer into the input remains valid only while that input buffer remains valid.

Positive input bases range from 2 through 62. Base zero requests prefix detection for binary and hexadecimal forms and otherwise selects decimal. The parser recognizes @ as a radix-exponent marker in every base, e or E in bases at most 10, and p or P as a binary-exponent marker in bases 2 and 16. These distinctions matter: a hexadecimal digit may itself be the letter e, so treating every e as an exponent marker would be ambiguous. Use an explicit base for a persistent text protocol, and define its special-value policy rather than accepting NaN or infinity accidentally.

Short input does not necessarily mean cheap input. A small exponent token can request a large exact radix power. The parser has construction limits and range checks, but an application accepting untrusted text should also bound input length, requested precision, and its own permitted exponent range. A resource rejection is a conversion failure to handle, not permission to use a partially computed value.

11.2 Digits and the separate exponent

ppf_get_str returns significand digits without a radix point. For an ordinary finite value, interpret the result as a fraction beginning immediately before the first digit, multiplied by the base raised to the returned exponent. The sign, when present, precedes the digits. Thus the five decimal digits 12500 and exponent 1 describe 0.12500 × 10, or 1.25. They do not describe the integer 12,500.

The digits argument requests the number of significant radix digits. Zero asks the library to choose a count from the object’s binary precision; ppf_get_str_ndigits exposes that sizing calculation. This choice is useful for general output, but a protocol should still specify its base and rounding policy. If exact binary text is required, base 2 with enough digits to retain the stored significand avoids an additional decimal rounding step. For a complete saved object, use the binary interchange interface below.

With buffer == NULL, the library allocates the string and retains the allocator provenance needed to release it. Call ppf_free_str exactly once. Do not pass that allocation to free. Conversely, a buffer supplied by the caller remains caller-owned and must not be passed to ppf_free_str merely because ppf_get_str wrote into it. The caller-buffer form has no capacity argument; allocated output is usually the easier choice unless storage bounds are already established.

Special values have token representations rather than an ordinary significand/exponent pair. Handle their categories explicitly when consuming the digits API. Do not interpret an exponent variable left from an earlier call as the exponent of NaN or infinity.

11.3 Formatting for people

The ppf_*printf family accepts ordinary C conversions, GMP conversions, and Polyphase floating conversions beginning with %R. Pass the address of the initialized ppf_t, not a copied structure or a C floating value. For example, "%.2RNf" prints two digits after the decimal point, using nearest rounding. The N belongs to the formatting conversion; it is not a change to the object’s stored precision or to the context’s default rounding mode.

Conversion Typical purpose
%Rf, %RF A fixed number of decimal places
%Re, %RE Scientific decimal notation
%Rg, %RG A compact decimal presentation
%Ra, %RA Hexadecimal floating notation
%Rb Binary floating notation
%Pu A ppf_prec_t value as an unsigned quantity

After R, the selectors N, Z, U, D, and Y request nearest, toward zero, toward positive infinity, toward negative infinity, and away from zero, respectively. A * selector consumes a rounding-mode argument immediately before the floating-object pointer. Ordinary dynamic field width and precision consume their own integer arguments in the usual order. Prefer a literal, simple format until those argument positions are familiar.

Choose ppf_snprintf for fixed-capacity buffers. Its nonnegative result is the length that would have been produced, excluding the terminating null byte. A result greater than or equal to the supplied capacity means truncation; it is not an allocation error. Test for a negative result before converting that result to an unsigned type. Choose ppf_asprintf when the required length is not known in advance. Its successful allocation must be released with ordinary free, and failure leaves its output pointer null.

Allocation source Required release
ppf_get_str(NULL, ...) ppf_free_str(text)
ppf_asprintf or ppf_vasprintf free(text)
Caller-supplied array No library release; follow the array’s own lifetime

Formatting interfaces without an explicit context use the calling thread’s default context for their internal diagnostics. Inspecting an unrelated explicit context will not explain their failure. Keep format strings under application control: pass user text through "%s", never as the format itself. Conversions such as %n and %Rn write through pointers. Their earlier side effects are not rolled back if a later conversion fails. Positional $ arguments are rejected. Large field widths can demand substantial work even when the final destination buffer is small, so bound user-selected widths and precisions before formatting.

11.4 Streams, locales, and commit boundaries

ppf_inp_str skips initial white space and reads a non-white-space token. ppf_out_str writes a formatted numeric token. A null input stream selects standard input; a null output stream selects standard output. Applications should normally pass their stream explicitly so an accidental null pointer does not redirect data to a terminal.

Do not confuse numerical rollback with stream rollback. Failed input may have consumed bytes while leaving the destination unchanged. Output staging can fail before any write, but once writing begins a short write or an I/O error can leave a prefix in the stream. Use application-level record framing, temporary files, and a checked file replacement when an entire saved document must be committed atomically. Check flushing and closing too: buffered output can report an error after a successful formatting call.

The text stream formatter consults the active locale’s decimal point. The number parser recognizes the library’s numeric syntax, including a dot radix point. Keep machine-readable text in the C locale with a defined grammar, or use PPFIF. Avoid changing process locale while other threads format data.

11.5 PPFIF records

The binary representation is called PPFIF01. It records value category, sign, binary precision, binary exponent, significand bytes in a defined byte order, and a CRC-32 check. It is independent of the in-memory limb layout and of host byte order. It is not MPFR’s experimental FPIF representation, and a raw dump of ppf_t is neither a PPFIF record nor a portable file.

Import restores the encoded precision as well as the value. It does not round the record into the destination’s previous precision. If an application needs a particular working precision or range, import into a temporary object, validate application-specific limits, and perform a separate rounded assignment into the working destination. Category policies also belong to the application: a valid NaN record can still be inappropriate for a price or a physical measurement.

The default importer bounds the encoded payload and the rounded-up significand storage independently at 64 MiB each. This also prevents a special record with no payload from requesting unlimited storage through a claimed precision. The private build macro PPF_FPIF_MAX_IMPORT_BYTES can change that positive construction bound. It is not a per-call memory budget, a limit on the total file size, or a guarantee of peak process memory. Oversized resource requests return -1, raise PPF_FLAG_ERANGE, and preserve the destination. Malformed, truncated, or checksum-invalid records likewise do not publish a partially decoded object. Not every malformed record necessarily raises the same flag; always check the return value.

A CRC detects accidental corruption; it does not authenticate a sender or protect against deliberate modification. Apply authentication and transport limits at the surrounding protocol layer when they are needed.

The complete example systems_io.c prints the digits and formatted value of 1.25, then exports and imports a PPFIF record through a temporary stream. It deliberately initializes the receiving object at a different precision and checks that import restores the stored precision. Its cleanup shows the two different string-release rules in one place.

12 Memory ownership and in-place operations

A ppf_t owns or refers to significand storage; a context owns mutable execution policy and reusable scratch space. Treat both as managed C objects with explicit lifetimes. The most reliable application structure initializes them once, checks each fallible call, and releases them through one cleanup path. That structure is also the foundation for safe in-place operations and for recovery from allocation failure.

12.1 Establish ownership before computing

For local numbers, zero-initialize the structure before a sequence of initialization calls. This allows a common cleanup path to call ppf_clear on objects whose initialization was never attempted. Successfully initialize the context before using it to initialize numbers. A failure to allocate a significand during valid ppf_init2_ctx initialization leaves a safe-zero object; it does not leave a usable numerical value.

ppf_context_t ctx;
ppf_t x = {0}, y = {0};

if (ppf_context_init(&ctx) != 0) return 1;
if (ppf_init2_ctx(&x, 128, &ctx) != 0 ||
    ppf_init2_ctx(&y, 128, &ctx) != 0) {
    ppf_clear(&y);
    ppf_clear(&x);
    ppf_context_clear(&ctx);
    return 1;
}
/* Assign values and perform checked calculations here. */
ppf_clear(&y);
ppf_clear(&x);
ppf_context_clear(&ctx);

Do not initialize an already live object again to change its precision. That can abandon its existing allocation. ppf_set_prec changes precision but discards the old value on success, leaving NaN. Use ppf_prec_round when retaining and rounding the old value is the intention. ppf_reserve reserves capacity; it is not itself a request to change the numerical precision or value.

Do not copy a live ppf_t with C structure assignment or memcpy. That copies the storage pointer and ownership metadata, so two apparent objects can refer to one allocation and later free it twice. Use ppf_set to assign a value into an initialized destination, and ppf_swap when ownership of two complete objects should be exchanged. Similarly, use ppf_context_clone to create a context with copied policy and its own initially empty scratch state; a raw copy can duplicate ownership of arena blocks.

12.2 Supplying an allocator

ppf_context_init_custom accepts a ppf_allocator_t containing allocation, reallocation, and release callbacks plus an opaque pointer. Supply all three callbacks. The reallocation callback receives old and new byte sizes; it must leave the old block valid when it returns null. The release callback receives the size associated with that allocation. Respect these sizes when integrating a pool, accounting system, or debugging allocator.

Objects retain the allocator needed to release their own significands. An allocated ppf_get_str result likewise retains allocator provenance. This does not extend the lifetime of the opaque application state. Keep that state, and any supporting pool or callback code, alive until every dependent number, string, arena, and other owned resource has been released. Clearing the context is not a substitute for clearing the numbers created through it.

The complete systems_allocation.c example uses a small allocator wrapper that can reject its next request. It first stores 37, forces the temporary-object allocation in ppf_set_str to fail, and checks that 37 remains stored. After clearing the allocation flag, a retry reads 1.25 successfully. The program also checks that all blocks allocated through the wrapper have been released. This is an example of the project allocator contract, not a simulation of every possible system-wide out-of-memory condition.

If several contexts share one allocator and opaque pointer, the allocator’s own synchronization must support the way those contexts are used. Separate contexts do not make a shared allocation counter or pool thread-safe.

12.3 What failure preserves

The library distinguishes initialization, assignment, and temporary resource construction. Their failure outcomes are useful only when the destination was valid and the function’s preconditions were met.

Operation class Useful failure rule
Significand allocation during ppf_init2_ctx The object is safe to clear; there is no previous value to preserve
Covered numerical transaction with an initialized destination An unrecovered project-allocation failure preserves that destination
ppf_reserve or ppf_set_prec reallocation Failure preserves the original object and allocation
Initializer followed by assignment A later setter failure may leave an initialized object that still needs clearing
Stream input The number can be preserved although input bytes were consumed
Stream output Staging can fail before writing; an I/O failure after writing starts can leave a prefix

PPF_FLAG_ALLOC is sticky. It says that a project-controlled allocation was refused; it does not by itself say that the operation failed. Some operations recover through an exact fallback and return a normal result with the flag still set. Check the function’s result first, then interpret the flag according to the application’s resource policy. For an isolated measurement, clear the flag on the same context before the operation. The short convenience flag functions inspect the thread-default context, which may be different from an explicit context passed to the calculation.

The transactional rule covers the specified project-allocation paths. It is not a general promise to preserve the old value for every numerical error. Domain errors, unresolved numerical certification, invalid arguments, and ordinary overflow have their own documented outcomes. Nor does it promise rollback of all externally visible state: flags can change, input streams can advance, and formatting %n conversions can already have written a count.

GMP allocations form a separate domain from ppf_context_t. A custom Polyphase allocator does not intercept every temporary integer or rational allocated by GMP. C-library stream buffering, some process allocations, and operating-system resources are separate too. Plan application memory limits with those domains in mind. Do not replace GMP’s process-level allocation functions casually inside an application that already has live GMP objects or other GMP users.

12.4 In-place arithmetic without accidental overlap

An in-place call such as ppf_add(&x, &x, &y, ...) means that one initialized object appears in an allowed destination and input position. It does not mean that unrelated objects may share arbitrary portions of their limb arrays. Consult the function’s aliasing classification when building a generic wrapper or using an unfamiliar operation; similarity between function names is not a storage contract.

Ordinary arithmetic families support their documented in-place cases. The destination’s precision still controls the rounded result, even when the destination is also an input. If different precision is needed for the result, create or prepare that destination explicitly rather than assuming an input’s precision will be inherited.

Multi-output operations need special attention. The two floating outputs of ppf_modf, ppf_sin_cos, and ppf_sinh_cosh must be distinct, although either may individually alias the input where the contract permits it. ppf_grandom also requires distinct floating outputs when both are present; its second output may instead be null. ppf_get_constant_interval requires distinct lower and upper GMP integer objects. Two pointer variables pointing to the same object are not distinct outputs.

For ppf_div_with_plan_many, a destination may coincide with its numerator at the same index. Duplicate destinations and cross-index destination/input overlap are rejected before the batch begins. This prevents a result written early in the batch from silently replacing an operand needed later. Check array relationships before submitting a batch, especially when arrays are assembled from slices or views.

Lifecycle functions are not ordinary in-place assignments. An initializer needs unused destination storage; initializing it from itself cannot preserve a value that initialization destroys. Direct-storage functions likewise have their own capacity, alignment, normalization, and overlap requirements.

12.5 Scratch space and caller-owned limbs

The context arena is useful when an integration needs temporary storage with a shared scope. Take a mark before allocations and release back to it after the temporary work. Growing the arena uses linked blocks and does not move earlier returned addresses. A failed growth request leaves the earlier block chain and mark usable. Restoring a mark ends the lifetime of allocations made after that mark; no saved pointer into those allocations may be used afterward.

ppf_arena_reset keeps reusable storage rather than necessarily returning every byte to the operating system. ppf_context_clear releases the context’s arena. Do not use an arena mark as a permanent bookmark across context cleanup, and do not mix marks from different contexts.

Advanced external-significand storage avoids ordinary ownership of limb memory. Its backing allocation must have enough capacity and remain valid while the object uses it. Clearing an externally backed object does not transfer ownership of that backing allocation to the library. Growing, relocating, or editing the buffer requires the appropriate direct-storage procedure; bypassing it can break normalization and expose readers to inconsistent data. Start with ordinary owned objects unless the integration has a measured need for direct storage and can enforce these lifetimes.

At shutdown, release returned strings and user-owned numbers, destroy plans and random states, clear explicit contexts, and then perform any desired thread-local cache cleanup. That order keeps allocator state alive until its dependents are gone and makes repeated computations easier to reason about.

13 Threads, runtime policy, and cache lifetime

The simplest concurrency arrangement gives each worker its own context and destination objects, while sharing only inputs that remain immutable until all workers finish. This arrangement works whether the library was built with internal OpenMP support or with its serial numerical paths. Application threads and internal numerical workers are separate layers of concurrency.

13.1 Share values, own mutations

Resource Concurrent-use rule
Initialized number used only as an input May be shared while its storage and value remain unchanged
Destination number Requires exclusive ownership during mutation
Explicit context Requires one-thread-at-a-time ownership or an application lock
Thread-default context Private to its calling thread
Completed divisor plan May be applied concurrently with separate destinations and contexts
GMP random state Requires exclusive ownership or an application lock
Constant and transcendental caches Internally synchronized; purges may wait for active users

An input is no longer read-only when another thread resizes it, swaps it, clears it, edits its limbs, or uses it as an aliased output. Keep those actions outside the readers’ lifetime. const ppf_t * helps express the intended use, but it cannot stop a different pointer from mutating the same object. The application must enforce the ownership rule.

An explicit context is mutable even when every numerical operand is read-only. An operation can update its flags or use its scratch arena. Passing one shared context to otherwise independent calculations therefore needs synchronization. Giving each worker a context is usually simpler than locking around every arithmetic call. If the workers need common settings, initialize their contexts from a stable policy or clone a context before starting the concurrent work. A clone copies flags as well as policy, so clear inherited flags when a clean diagnostic interval is wanted.

The complete systems_threads.c example starts two POSIX threads. They both read one initialized value, 7, and independently square it into private destinations. Each checks that its result is 49. Only the main thread prints, after joining both workers, so the example’s output is deterministic. The shared input is cleared after the joins. The same pattern scales to a larger worker pool: worker-local context, local output, immutable shared input, and an explicit completion boundary.

13.2 Default contexts and flags

The convenience default context is thread-local. Changing one thread’s default precision, exponent range, rounding mode, or flags does not change another thread’s defaults. This is useful for a small program, but it also means that a worker cannot report its numerical flags merely by having the main thread inspect the main thread’s default context.

Collect the status and flags in the worker that performed the operation, then publish an application result record after the work is complete. Such a record can contain the operation status, a copied flag mask, and the resulting value or a reference whose ownership is transferred to the receiving thread. Do not publish a pointer to a worker’s stack-allocated context or to an object that the worker clears before the receiver finishes reading it.

Formatting functions without a context argument use the calling thread’s default context. A worker using an explicit numerical context can therefore have two relevant diagnostic sources: its explicit calculation context and the default context used for formatting. Keeping presentation in a separate stage can make this distinction easier to manage.

13.3 Choosing the level of parallelism

The CMake option PPF_OPENMP accepts OFF, ON, and AUTO. OFF builds without the OpenMP runtime dependency. ON requires usable OpenMP support for the chosen compiler. AUTO enables support when the compiler and runtime probe succeeds. These options do not change the ownership rules for objects, contexts, or custom allocator state.

Operations exposing a worker-count argument receive a request, not a promise to launch that many workers. The selected algorithm may have fewer useful tasks; small inputs may use a serial route; and nested parallel execution can be limited. A request of many workers is therefore not evidence that the operation used the whole machine. Consult operation statistics where the interface provides them and retain the build configuration when measuring parallel behavior.

The constant-family default worker setting is process-wide and atomic. The trigonometric default worker preference is thread-local. Configure these preferences deliberately, preferably before the relevant workload starts. Changing a process-wide preference during a timing campaign makes the campaign harder to interpret even when the change is safely synchronized. Explicit worker-count forms are useful when one call needs a policy different from the surrounding application’s default.

Avoid oversubscription. For a server processing many independent requests, several application workers each requesting a large OpenMP team may compete for the same cores and memory bandwidth. Begin with one parallel layer, then measure whether nested or mixed execution improves the actual workload. A throughput-oriented server and a single very-high-precision calculation can need different policies. Neither a worker count nor an environment setting alone guarantees CPU affinity or exclusive access to a core.

13.4 Reproducible results and reproducible execution

Specify precision, rounding mode, exponent range, and input values explicitly when reproducibility matters. Record the library and dependency builds too. Numerical reproducibility is different from repeating the same algorithm, cache state, schedule, allocation count, or elapsed time. A planner can choose an exact computational route that differs from another route while producing the same rounded numerical result.

Faithful rounding needs particular care: its contract permits an allowed neighboring result rather than the unique result selected by a specified directed or nearest mode. Do not use a byte-for-byte comparison across implementations as the sole validity test for faithful rounding. Likewise, special-function acceptance remains subject to documented precision and construction limits; a worker policy is not a guarantee that every possible input can be certified within those limits.

For randomized calculations, keep a separate initialized GMP random state per worker or lock a shared state. Choose and record the seeding scheme at the application level. Reusing the same seed independently in every worker can produce repeated streams, which may be undesirable even though the calls are free of data races. Thread scheduling should not silently determine the meaning of a reproducible experiment’s sample numbering.

13.5 Cache reuse and cleanup

Caches reduce repeated construction work for constants and related calculations. They also retain memory after an individual function returns. That retained memory is not automatically a leak: it can be intentionally owned by a cache or a reusable thread workspace. Distinguish an increasing unreachable allocation from a stable reusable allocation before changing an application’s memory policy.

ppf_clear_constant_cache releases a selected constant’s cached value; ppf_free_constant_caches clears the constant caches collectively. ppf_free_cache2(PPF_FREE_GLOBAL_CACHE) covers the global-cache cleanup interface. Purging shared caches is supported while other threads calculate, but it takes the corresponding locks and may block. A later call can rebuild what was removed. Periodic purging in a latency-sensitive request path can therefore make both that request and subsequent requests slower.

ppf_free_cache2(PPF_FREE_LOCAL_CACHE) affects the calling thread’s local scratch pool and product workspaces. It cannot release another live worker’s local storage. If workers retain large temporary workspaces, schedule local cleanup in those workers at a sensible boundary, such as after an unusually large job or when returning a worker to an idle pool.

ppf_thread_cleanup provides explicit cleanup of heap-backed state owned by the calling thread and may be called repeatedly. On the POSIX baseline, ordinary thread exit also performs cleanup when the thread-specific destructor key was successfully registered. ppf_buildopt_thread_cleanup_p reports that key’s availability. Explicit cleanup remains useful for controlled shutdown, for the main thread, and before unloading the library.

Thread cleanup does not destroy application-owned numbers, explicit contexts, divisor plans, or GMP random states. Clear those resources through their own lifecycle interfaces. Before unloading a shared library, stop new calls, wait for active workers to finish, release their resources and local state, and only then unload it. Automatic thread cleanup cannot make a callback into an already unloaded library safe.

Use runtime identity functions such as ppf_get_version, ppf_abi_tag, and the build-option queries when constructing a diagnostic report. They help identify the library actually loaded, which can differ from a header found first on the compiler’s include path. Keep these diagnostics separate from numerical output that another program expects to parse.

14 Application integration and performance measurement

Integrate the installed library first, then tune a representative workload. This sequence separates packaging mistakes from numerical mistakes and gives measurements a clear dependency configuration. The production core uses GMP for integer machinery and does not require MPFR. The optional MPFR adapter is a separate library for applications that need that boundary.

14.1 Build an installation you can identify

Use CMake for an installed package. A serial core build is a useful starting point because it has fewer optional dependencies and is easy to reproduce:

cmake -S . -B build/core \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DPPF_OPENMP=OFF \
  -DPPF_MPFR_SUPPORT=OFF
cmake --build build/core -j2
cmake --install build/core --prefix "$HOME/.local"

Run these commands from the Polyphase source directory. -j2 controls build parallelism, not the number of workers used by a numerical operation. The installation prefix is an application deployment choice; it need not be the example shown here. On the supported Linux baseline, development headers and libraries for GMP, a C11 compiler, POSIX threads, and the platform math library are required. Install the development files for the architecture actually being compiled, rather than relying only on a runtime shared library.

Both shared and static library forms are normally built. Use PPF_BUILD_SHARED=OFF or PPF_BUILD_STATIC=OFF when only one form is wanted, leaving at least one enabled. Use a fresh build directory when changing the compiler, sanitizer configuration, or major dependency settings. A stale CMake cache can otherwise continue to select an old compiler or dependency path despite changes in the shell environment.

Native instruction tuning is disabled by default. Enable PPF_ENABLE_NATIVE_OPTIMIZATIONS only when the deployment machines support the instructions selected for the build machine. A binary that performs well locally but fails with an illegal instruction on a recipient’s computer is not a successful portable optimization.

14.2 Consume exported CMake targets

In a separate application directory, use an installed package rather than copying internal source files into the application:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.23)
project(polyphase_application LANGUAGES C)
find_package(PolyphaseFloat CONFIG REQUIRED COMPONENTS core)
add_executable(polyphase_application main.c)
target_link_libraries(polyphase_application PRIVATE PolyphaseFloat::shared)

Set CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH to the installation prefix when configuring that application. It should not point at the Polyphase source tree. The exported target supplies include paths and its declared link dependencies. Select PolyphaseFloat::static for the archive form, provided that form was installed. This is preferable to maintaining a handwritten list of transitive dependencies for each OpenMP and platform configuration.

Request COMPONENTS core when the application does not use MPFR. An unqualified package request can load an installed adapter as well. Request COMPONENTS mpfr when the adapter is required; the package then loads the core and exposes the installed PolyphaseFloat::mpfr_shared and/or PolyphaseFloat::mpfr_static targets. A missing required component should fail configuration early instead of becoming an unexplained link error later.

An installed header being found does not prove that the intended library is loaded at runtime. Configure the platform loader for the installed shared library directory using the application’s deployment policy. Build-tree runtime paths are convenient during development but are not a replacement for a distributable application’s installation layout. When diagnosing an unexpected version, compare runtime identity with the headers and package configuration selected during compilation.

14.3 Using pkg-config or Make

The core package name is polyphase-float; the adapter package name is polyphase-float-mpfr. For a small application with installed dependencies:

cc -std=c11 main.c -o my_app \
  $(pkg-config --cflags --libs polyphase-float)

If the prefix is outside the system search path, add the directory containing the installed .pc files to PKG_CONFIG_PATH. Library directories can be nested or architecture-specific; use the actual installation layout instead of assuming that every system installs into a directory literally named lib. The installed pkg-config metadata is designed to follow a relocated complete prefix when relative install directories are used.

pkg-config --static --libs polyphase-float adds the private dependency flags needed by static linking. It does not itself force the linker to select an archive when a shared library is also available. Use the explicit CMake static target, a static-only installation, or a deliberate linker selection when that distinction matters. Fully static linking of all system dependencies is a separate platform question from selecting Polyphase’s static archive.

The source Makefile supports development commands such as make test, make audit, and named bin/ targets. CMake is the canonical installation route. Keep independent compiler or sanitizer builds in separate directories or clean copies; reusing old objects with different instrumentation can produce misleading failures. A successful source-tree test does not by itself exercise downstream discovery of an installed package.

14.4 Crossing the MPFR boundary

Build and install the adapter with official MPFR development headers when an application needs <polyphase_float_mpfr.h>. Some local validation modes can use a minimal compatibility declaration set with an existing MPFR shared library. That arrangement does not supply the installable adapter contract for downstream applications. Prefer an explicit PPF_MPFR_SUPPORT=ON when the adapter is required, so missing development dependencies are reported at configuration time.

The three conversion directions have distinct precision policies:

Interface Precision policy Return convention
ppf_import_mpfr_exact Adopts the MPFR source precision for exact import 0 on success, -1 on failure
ppf_set_mpfr Keeps the initialized Polyphase destination precision and applies the requested rounding and context range Numerical ternary; check PPF_TERNARY_ERROR before its sign
ppf_get_mpfr Rounds into the initialized MPFR destination’s precision using an MPFR rounding mode MPFR numerical ternary

All arguments must be valid, and destinations must satisfy their respective initialization requirements. A return value is not a substitute for these preconditions. Exact import may change the destination precision before a later failure; it does not promise to preserve the previous destination on every failure. Check the function-specific return convention rather than assuming that every adapter call returns the same kind of status. MPFR’s own flags and exponent policy remain part of the MPFR side of the boundary. A Polyphase context is not a replacement for MPFR’s runtime state.

The adapter also provides two enumeration translators: ppf_rounding_from_mpfr maps an MPFR rounding mode to its corresponding Polyphase mode, and ppf_rounding_to_mpfr maps in the opposite direction. Both translate the six concrete modes: nearest, toward zero, upward, downward, away from zero, and faithful. Both fall back to nearest for an unrecognized value; they do not return an error indicator. In particular, ppf_rounding_to_mpfr(PPF_RND_DEFAULT) yields MPFR_RNDN. It does not consult a Polyphase context. If the intended policy is a context’s current default, resolve that policy to its concrete rounding mode before translating it.

The complete systems_mpfr_bridge.c example imports an exact MPFR value 5/4, verifies adoption of its 128-bit precision, multiplies by 8 in Polyphase, and exports the exact result 10 to a 53-bit MPFR destination. The small exact values make the example’s precision changes visible without confusing them with unavoidable rounding.

For migration of a larger calculation, convert at a well-defined boundary, perform a substantial sequence of operations in one representation, and convert back when needed. Alternating representations at every elementary operation can add allocation, conversion, and repeated-rounding costs. Measure the complete application path if frequent conversion is unavoidable. Do not attribute all of that path’s cost to either arithmetic engine alone.

14.5 Make the workload stable before tuning

Start by reusing initialized objects and choosing realistic working precisions. Repeated initialization and teardown inside a tight loop may dominate a small arithmetic operation. Separate object setup, cache warmup, plan construction, and timed application according to what the real workload does. A reusable divisor plan is valuable only when enough applications amortize its construction and storage costs.

Preserve the intended numerical calculation while optimizing it. A fused operation and a sequence with an intermediate rounding are different computations. Choosing fewer printed digits improves presentation costs but does not reduce the precision of an already computed result. Likewise, raising a worker count is a scheduling request, not an assurance of lower latency. Record which question a measurement is intended to answer before changing several variables at once.

The portable product planner selects algorithms from operation, size, and worker conditions. Optional machine-specific profiles can change those choices; explicit algorithm requests have their own selection semantics. Keep any custom profile with the build record. A profile chosen on one CPU or one cache-placement policy is not automatically suitable for another.

14.6 Interpret measurements at their actual scope

A useful timing record identifies the operation, inputs or generation rule, precision, rounding mode, worker count, build flags, dependency builds, hardware, and correctness check. Retain raw samples rather than only a best time. State whether the result measures a cold call, a warmed cache, a planned application, or an end-to-end task including setup and conversion.

Compare equal questions. A many-worker latency measurement and a one-worker measurement answer a scaling question; they are not automatically an equal-resource throughput comparison. Include plan construction when claiming benefit for a one-off division. Include output formatting when the application spends most of its time writing results. If system load or CPU placement changes between runs, an observed difference may have several causes.

The repository’s benchmark pipeline retains correctness-gated samples and uses independent process launches as the experimental units. Multiple samples inside one process describe that process’s variability; they do not establish independent reproducibility. A correctness gate checks the tested values and conditions, not every mathematical input. Report performance as a result for the measured configuration and workload, with its uncertainty and omitted costs stated. No benchmark smoke test alone establishes a general speedup.

15 Troubleshooting and diagnostic workflow

Begin with the failing call, its actual return convention, and the context used by that call. Record the input values and their precisions before changing code or increasing precision. Many apparent arithmetic failures are caused by reading the wrong flags, changing a destination’s precision in a way that discards its value, or loading a library different from the one used at compile time.

15.1 First distinguish status from rounding

An arithmetic ternary result is negative when the stored result lies below the exact result, zero when exact, and positive when above, subject to the operation’s documented special cases. PPF_TERNARY_ERROR is a distinct error sentinel. Therefore a condition such as if (ppf_add(...)) treats ordinary inexact arithmetic as failure. Check the sentinel first, then interpret the ternary relation if needed.
